Ōmiwa Jinja served as the sōja of that kokufu, and the local place name “Sōja” is derived from this shrine.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.city.tochigi.lg.jp/uploaded/attachment/55689.pdf|title=Chapter 2: Historical Scenery of Tochigi City to be Maintained and Improved |website=Tochigi City|accessdate=2024-11-11|page=177}}</ref>
The shrine is also known for the "Muro no Yashima" (Muro no Yashima) mentioned in Matsuo Bashō’s famous travelogue, the "Oku no Hosomichi."
== Deities Enshrined == '''Principal deity:''' * *Yamato-Ōmononushi-Kushi-mikatama no Mikoto* (倭大物主櫛𤭖玉命)<ref>According to the shrine's official literature.</ref> : In the "Izumo no Kuni no Miyatsuko Kamuyogoto," this refers to Ōmononushi no Kami. The deity is said to be an offshoot of the Ōmiwa Jinja (大神神社) in Sakurai City, Nara Prefecture. During Emperor Sujin’s reign, suffering from natural disasters and plagues, the emperor had a dream in which the deity Ōmononushi appeared and gave instructions. Following them, a man named Ootataneko performed rites at Mount Miwa, resulting in the cessation of calamities and epidemics. This story is recorded in the "Nihon Shoki."
'''Additional Deities (Aiadono-matsuri):''' * Kono-hanasakuya-hime (木花咲耶姫命) * Ninigi no Mikoto (瓊々杵命), husband of Kono-hanasakuya-hime * Ōyamatsumi no Mikoto (大山祇命), father of Kono-hanasakuya-hime * Hikohohodemi no Mikoto (彦火々出見命), child of Kono-hanasakuya-hime
== History == === Founding === According to shrine tradition, during Emperor Sujin's era, Prince Toyokiirihiko (豊城入彦命), while subjugating the eastern provinces, prayed for victory and peace of mind at a place known as "Muro no Yashima." He is said to have enshrined the great deity of Ōmiwa (from the capital at Isonokami in Yamato) at this site, establishing the shrine.<ref name="由緒書">Shrine’s official literature.</ref>
=== Historical Overview === The mid-Heian period text "Engishiki Jinmyōchō" lists a “Ōgami Jinja” in Tsuga District, Shimotsuke Province. One theory identifies Ōmiwa Jinja with that shrine, making it a "ronsha" (disputed match).<ref>Another candidate is Taihei-san Jinja in Hirai-chō, Tochigi City.</ref>
In ancient times, provincial governors (kokushi) would visit all shrines in the province, starting with the ichinomiya. To streamline this, they established a sōja near the kokufu to collectively worship all regional deities. Ōmiwa Jinja is believed to have served as the sōja of Shimotsuke Province. About 2.8 km south, the ruins of the Shimotsuke Kokuchō (provincial government offices) have been excavated.
During the rebellion of Taira no Masakado (Heian period), the shrine suffered damage. Fujiwara no Hidesato and others helped rebuild it, and until the Muromachi period, it had grand buildings.<ref name="由緒書"/> However, during the Sengoku period, the remnants of Minagawa Hiroteru’s forces barricaded themselves in the shrine. Hōjō Ujinao’s army set it on fire, resulting in destruction and decline.<ref name="由緒書"/>
It was said that through contributions by Tokugawa Iemitsu, who donated 30 koku of land and 10,000 pine saplings, the shrine was rebuilt in 1682 (Tenna 2) to its current form.<ref name="由緒書"/>
However, no historical documents prior to the Meiji era have been found that clearly refer to this shrine as “Ōmiwa (Ōmiwa)” or “Ōmiwa.” One theory suggests that a deity from Ōmiwa Jinja (Ōmiwa Jinja in Yamato) was worshiped at another location and later merged at the Sōja of Shimotsuke.<ref>On-site information board.</ref>
After the Meiji Restoration, in Meiji 6 (1873), the shrine was Ranked as a Gōsha (village shrine) under the modern shrine Ranking system.<ref name="由緒書"/> In Meiji 40 (1907), it was designated a shrine entitled to government offerings (Shinsen Heihaku Ryō Kyōshin Jinja), and in Meiji 44 (1911), it was promoted to Prefectural Shrine. Major renovations took place in 1924 (Taishō 13) and 1993 (Heisei 5). The Kuniho family traditionally served as hereditary Ōmiya-gūji (chief priests).
=== Shinhonors (Shinkai)=== * On August 29, Genkei 4 (880), it was elevated from Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade to Senior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade in the "Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku." The recorded deity name is "Miwa no Kami (三和神)"—some believe this refers to this shrine.<ref name="地名">"Tochigi-ken no Chimei" (Heibonsha) entry on Ōmiwa Jinja.</ref>
== Precincts == === Shrine Buildings === <gallery widths="200px" heights="150px"> File:Oomiwa-jinja (tochigishi) honden.JPG|Honden File:Oomiwa-jinja (tochigishi) haiden.JPG|Haiden File:Oomiwa-jinja (tochigishi) kaguraden.JPG|Kagura-den </gallery>
=== Sanctuary Forest === The forested area around Ōmiwa Jinja is designated as the Sōja Greenery Conservation Area by Tochigi Prefecture.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.pref.tochigi.lg.jp/d04/30jikannti/12souja.html|title=12 Sōja Greenery Environmental Conservation Area|website=Tochigi Prefecture|accessdate=2024-11-11}}</ref>
=== Muro no Yashima === [[File:Oomiwa-jinja (tochigishi) muronoyashima.JPG|thumb|200px|Muro no Yashima]] [[File:TochigiOhmiwaShine2.JPG|thumb|200px|Bashō’s haiku monument before Muro no Yashima]] "Muro no Yashima" has long been known as a utamakura (poetic place name) in classical Japanese poetry. The island in the shrine’s pond is said to be its location (though some argue this is a later association).<ref>See Kōjien, "Muro no Yashima." (Kotobank [https://kotobank.jp/word/%E5%AE%A4%E3%81%AE%E5%85%AB%E5%B3%B6-642624 article])</ref> It has been mentioned since the Nara period and appears in anthologies like the "Man’yōshū" and "Kokin Wakashū."
Famous poems: * Fujiwara no Sanekata (Shika Wakashū) * Minamoto no Shigeyuki’s daughter (Zoku Goshūi Wakashū) * Ōe no Masafusa (Shinshūi Wakashū) * Fujiwara no Shunzei (Chōshū Eiso) * Fujiwara no Teika (Shin Chokusen Wakashū)
Meanings associated with Muro no Yashima: * A site of a myth where Konohanasakuya-hime proved her chastity by setting herself aflame inside a room. * Possibly relates to a hearth’s smoke, turning into metaphorical love’s burning flame. * The marshy Omoigawa River basin producing water vapor or rising mist. * Over time associated with passionate love, smoke, and even kagerō (heat haze or spider’s thread).
Matsuo Bashō and his companion Sora mention Muro no Yashima in "Oku no Hosomichi," but they did not include a haiku in the main text. However, in Sora’s “Haikai Kakinotame,” one of Bashō’s verses “ito asobi ni musubitsukitaru keburi kana” ("Oh, the smoke that has tied itself to the thread playing in the air!") is recorded. This haiku is inscribed on a monument erected in 1869 (Meiji 2) by the late Edo period haijin Kōun Kaku Shunpō, with calligraphy by Hagiwara Shūgan, an Edo-period calligrapher.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Tochigi Inishie no Kairō: History of Cultural Properties |url=https://www.inishie.tochigi.jp/detail.html?course_id=5&id=0|accessdate=2024-02-22}}</ref>
Today’s Muro no Yashima is about 800 tsubo (approx. 2,640 square meters) of landscaped garden featuring eight small islands with small shrines dedicated to various prominent deities, including Tsukuba, Tenman, Kashima, Raiden, Sengen, Kumano, Futarayama, and Katori. There is no visible water vapor or spring water.
== Subordinate Shrines == [[File:Oomiwa-jinja (tochigishi) jingu.JPG|thumb|200px|Jingū: houses the aidadono (shared) deities of the main shrine]] There are 15 shrine buildings in total:
{{div col}} * Jingū * Gokoku Jinja * Fukujin Jinja * Ōsugi Jinja * Soreisha * Samon Jinja * Umon Jinja {{div col end}}
'''Muro no Yashima''' {{div col}} * Sengen Jinja * Futarayama Jinja * Tsukuba Jinja * Raiden Jinja * Katori Jinja * Kashima Jinja * Kumano Jinja * Tenman-gū {{div col end}}
== festivals == * Gantan-sai (January 1st) * New Year’s Pilgrimage and Shinshun Kigan-sai (January) * Setsubun-sai and Tsuina-shiki (February 3rd) * Kinen-sai (February 25th) * Chinka-sai (Early March) * Spring Grand festival (April 16th) - Includes yabusame (horseback archery) * Hatsu-uma-sai (on the first Uma day in May) * Ōharae (June 30th) * Yashima-sai (August 1st) * Ōsugi-sai, Kaze-matsuri (Mid-August) * Shichi-go-san visits (November 15th) * Autumn Grand festival (Mikoshi festival) (around November 18-24)
== Cultural Properties == === Tochigi City Designated Intangible Folk Cultural Properties === * Kagura of Ōmiwa Jinja - designated May 19, 1964 * Hoko (Spear) festival of Ōmiwa Jinja - designated May 19, 1964
=== Historic Sites === * Tochigi City Designated Historic Site "Shimotsuke Sōja (Muro no Yashima)" - designated February 16, 1968
== location == * location: Sōja-chō 477, Tochigi City, Tochigi Prefecture == Access == * About 15 minutes’ walk from Yashū-Ōtsuka Station on the Tōbu Utsunomiya Line
== Surrounding Area == * Shimotsuke Kokuchō Ruins approx. 2.8 km south

{{Distinguish|Omiwa Shrine}} {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | image = File:Oomiwa-jinja (tochigishi) torii.JPG | deity = {{ill|Ōmononushi|qid=Q10936701}} | type = [[Sōja shrine|Sōja shrine]] |religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Ōmiwa Jinja (Oomiwa Shrine) | caption = | map_type = Japan Tochigi | coordinates = {{Coord|36.4059167|N|139.7821556|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | location = Sōja-chō 477, [[:en:Tochigi (city)|Tochigi City]], [[:en:Tochigi Prefecture|Tochigi Prefecture]] | type = Shikinaisha (small), a disputed identification (ronsha), Sōja of Shimotsuke Province, Former Prefectural Shrine | founded = (Trad.) 48th year of Emperor Sujin’s reign | festival = November 18–26 | location = {{ill|Tochigi|qid=Q44830}} }} {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine (Shimotsuke)|lt=Ōmiwa Jinja|ja|大神神社 (栃木市)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōmiwa Shrine (Shimotsuke)|qq=}} is a [[Sōja shrine|Sōja shrine]]. It enshrines all the [[kami]] of the shrines in [[:en:Shimotsuke Province|Shimotsuke Province]]
Ichinomiya and Soja are not the same thing but were sometimes combined<ref>https://archive.ph/wip/XtZfZ</ref>
{{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to a whole [[:en:Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[:en:Nara period|Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.<ref name="Herbert">{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}}</ref>
Whenever a new [[:en:Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,<ref name="Bocking">{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}}</ref>
The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[:en:Inaba|Inaba]]. <ref name="Hardacre">{{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}}</ref>
The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[:en:Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[:en:Okayama Prefecture|Okayama Prefecture]].

{{Distinguish|Omiwa Shrine}} {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | image = File:Oomiwa-jinja (tochigishi) torii.JPG | deity = {{ill|Ōmononushi|qid=Q10936701}} | type = [[Sōja shrine|Sōja shrine]] |religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Ōmiwa Jinja (Oomiwa Shrine) | caption = | map_type = Japan Tochigi | coordinates = {{Coord|36.4059167|N|139.7821556|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | location = Sōja-chō 477, [[:en:Tochigi (city)|Tochigi City]], [[:en:Tochigi Prefecture|Tochigi Prefecture]] | type = Shikinaisha (small), a disputed identification (ronsha), Sōja of Shimotsuke Province, Former Prefectural Shrine | founded = (Trad.) 48th year of Emperor Sujin’s reign | festival = November 18–26 | location = {{ill|Tochigi|qid=Q44830}} }} {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine (Shimotsuke)|lt=Ōmiwa Jinja|ja|大神神社 (栃木市)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōmiwa Shrine (Shimotsuke)|qq=}} is a [[Sōja shrine|Sōja shrine]]. It enshrines all the [[kami]] of the shrines in [[:en:Shimotsuke Province|Shimotsuke Province]]
Ichinomiya and Soja are not the same thing but were sometimes combined<ref>https://archive.ph/wip/XtZfZ</ref>
{{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to a whole [[:en:Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[:en:Nara period|Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.<ref name="Herbert">{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}}</ref>
Whenever a new [[:en:Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,<ref name="Bocking">{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}}</ref>
The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[:en:Inaba|Inaba]]. <ref name="Hardacre">{{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}}</ref>
The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[:en:Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[:en:Okayama Prefecture|Okayama Prefecture]].
==Japanese content== '''Ōmiwa Jinja''' (大神神社, also romanized as Oomiwa Jinja) is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] located in Sōja-chō, [[:en:Tochigi (city)|Tochigi City]], [[:en:Tochigi Prefecture|Tochigi Prefecture]], Japan. It is a possible match (ronsha) for a "Shikinaisha" (small) recorded in historical texts, and is known as the Sōja (total shrine) of Shimotsuke Province. Under the modern shrine Rank system of the Meiji era, it was classified as a Prefectural Shrine. Historically, it was also known by other names such as "Shimotsuke Sōja Daimyōjin," "Sōja Rokusho Daimyōjin," and "Muroyashima Sōja Daimyōjin."
During the Ritsuryō era, the provincial capital (kokufu) was located about 2 km south of the shrine. Ōmiwa Jinja served as the sōja of that kokufu, and the local place name “Sōja” is derived from this shrine.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.city.tochigi.lg.jp/uploaded/attachment/55689.pdf|title=Chapter 2: Historical Scenery of Tochigi City to be Maintained and Improved |website=Tochigi City|accessdate=2024-11-11|page=177}}</ref>
The shrine is also known for the "Muro no Yashima" (Muro no Yashima) mentioned in Matsuo Bashō’s famous travelogue, the "Oku no Hosomichi."
== Deities Enshrined == '''Principal deity:''' * *Yamato-Ōmononushi-Kushi-mikatama no Mikoto* (倭大物主櫛𤭖玉命)<ref>According to the shrine's official literature.</ref> : In the "Izumo no Kuni no Miyatsuko Kamuyogoto," this refers to Ōmononushi no Kami. The deity is said to be an offshoot of the Ōmiwa Jinja (大神神社) in Sakurai City, Nara Prefecture. During Emperor Sujin’s reign, suffering from natural disasters and plagues, the emperor had a dream in which the deity Ōmononushi appeared and gave instructions. Following them, a man named Ootataneko performed rites at Mount Miwa, resulting in the cessation of calamities and epidemics. This story is recorded in the "Nihon Shoki."
'''Additional Deities (Aiadono-matsuri):''' * Kono-hanasakuya-hime (木花咲耶姫命) * Ninigi no Mikoto (瓊々杵命), husband of Kono-hanasakuya-hime * Ōyamatsumi no Mikoto (大山祇命), father of Kono-hanasakuya-hime * Hikohohodemi no Mikoto (彦火々出見命), child of Kono-hanasakuya-hime
== History == === Founding === According to shrine tradition, during Emperor Sujin's era, Prince Toyokiirihiko (豊城入彦命), while subjugating the eastern provinces, prayed for victory and peace of mind at a place known as "Muro no Yashima." He is said to have enshrined the great deity of Ōmiwa (from the capital at Isonokami in Yamato) at this site, establishing the shrine.<ref name="由緒書">Shrine’s official literature.</ref>
=== Historical Overview === The mid-Heian period text "Engishiki Jinmyōchō" lists a “Ōgami Jinja” in Tsuga District, Shimotsuke Province. One theory identifies Ōmiwa Jinja with that shrine, making it a "ronsha" (disputed match).<ref>Another candidate is Taihei-san Jinja in Hirai-chō, Tochigi City.</ref>
In ancient times, provincial governors (kokushi) would visit all shrines in the province, starting with the ichinomiya. To streamline this, they established a sōja near the kokufu to collectively worship all regional deities. Ōmiwa Jinja is believed to have served as the sōja of Shimotsuke Province. About 2.8 km south, the ruins of the Shimotsuke Kokuchō (provincial government offices) have been excavated.
During the rebellion of Taira no Masakado (Heian period), the shrine suffered damage. Fujiwara no Hidesato and others helped rebuild it, and until the Muromachi period, it had grand buildings.<ref name="由緒書"/> However, during the Sengoku period, the remnants of Minagawa Hiroteru’s forces barricaded themselves in the shrine. Hōjō Ujinao’s army set it on fire, resulting in destruction and decline.<ref name="由緒書"/>
It was said that through contributions by Tokugawa Iemitsu, who donated 30 koku of land and 10,000 pine saplings, the shrine was rebuilt in 1682 (Tenna 2) to its current form.<ref name="由緒書"/>
However, no historical documents prior to the Meiji era have been found that clearly refer to this shrine as “Ōmiwa (Ōmiwa)” or “Ōmiwa.” One theory suggests that a deity from Ōmiwa Jinja (Ōmiwa Jinja in Yamato) was worshiped at another location and later merged at the Sōja of Shimotsuke.<ref>On-site information board.</ref>
After the Meiji Restoration, in Meiji 6 (1873), the shrine was Ranked as a Gōsha (village shrine) under the modern shrine Ranking system.<ref name="由緒書"/> In Meiji 40 (1907), it was designated a shrine entitled to government offerings (Shinsen Heihaku Ryō Kyōshin Jinja), and in Meiji 44 (1911), it was promoted to Prefectural Shrine. Major renovations took place in 1924 (Taishō 13) and 1993 (Heisei 5). The Kuniho family traditionally served as hereditary Ōmiya-gūji (chief priests).
=== Shinhonors (Shinkai)=== * On August 29, Genkei 4 (880), it was elevated from Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade to Senior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade in the "Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku." The recorded deity name is "Miwa no Kami (三和神)"—some believe this refers to this shrine.<ref name="地名">"Tochigi-ken no Chimei" (Heibonsha) entry on Ōmiwa Jinja.</ref>
== Precincts == === Shrine Buildings === <gallery widths="200px" heights="150px"> File:Oomiwa-jinja (tochigishi) honden.JPG|Honden File:Oomiwa-jinja (tochigishi) haiden.JPG|Haiden File:Oomiwa-jinja (tochigishi) kaguraden.JPG|Kagura-den </gallery>
=== Sanctuary Forest === The forested area around Ōmiwa Jinja is designated as the Sōja Greenery Conservation Area by Tochigi Prefecture.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.pref.tochigi.lg.jp/d04/30jikannti/12souja.html|title=12 Sōja Greenery Environmental Conservation Area|website=Tochigi Prefecture|accessdate=2024-11-11}}</ref>
=== Muro no Yashima === [[File:Oomiwa-jinja (tochigishi) muronoyashima.JPG|thumb|200px|Muro no Yashima]] [[File:TochigiOhmiwaShine2.JPG|thumb|200px|Bashō’s haiku monument before Muro no Yashima]] "Muro no Yashima" has long been known as a utamakura (poetic place name) in classical Japanese poetry. The island in the shrine’s pond is said to be its location (though some argue this is a later association).<ref>See Kōjien, "Muro no Yashima." (Kotobank [https://kotobank.jp/word/%E5%AE%A4%E3%81%AE%E5%85%AB%E5%B3%B6-642624 article])</ref> It has been mentioned since the Nara period and appears in anthologies like the "Man’yōshū" and "Kokin Wakashū."
Famous poems: * Fujiwara no Sanekata (Shika Wakashū) * Minamoto no Shigeyuki’s daughter (Zoku Goshūi Wakashū) * Ōe no Masafusa (Shinshūi Wakashū) * Fujiwara no Shunzei (Chōshū Eiso) * Fujiwara no Teika (Shin Chokusen Wakashū)
Meanings associated with Muro no Yashima: * A site of a myth where Konohanasakuya-hime proved her chastity by setting herself aflame inside a room. * Possibly relates to a hearth’s smoke, turning into metaphorical love’s burning flame. * The marshy Omoigawa River basin producing water vapor or rising mist. * Over time associated with passionate love, smoke, and even kagerō (heat haze or spider’s thread).
Matsuo Bashō and his companion Sora mention Muro no Yashima in "Oku no Hosomichi," but they did not include a haiku in the main text. However, in Sora’s “Haikai Kakinotame,” one of Bashō’s verses “ito asobi ni musubitsukitaru keburi kana” ("Oh, the smoke that has tied itself to the thread playing in the air!") is recorded. This haiku is inscribed on a monument erected in 1869 (Meiji 2) by the late Edo period haijin Kōun Kaku Shunpō, with calligraphy by Hagiwara Shūgan, an Edo-period calligrapher.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Tochigi Inishie no Kairō: History of Cultural Properties |url=https://www.inishie.tochigi.jp/detail.html?course_id=5&id=0|accessdate=2024-02-22}}</ref>
Today’s Muro no Yashima is about 800 tsubo (approx. 2,640 square meters) of landscaped garden featuring eight small islands with small shrines dedicated to various prominent deities, including Tsukuba, Tenman, Kashima, Raiden, Sengen, Kumano, Futarayama, and Katori. There is no visible water vapor or spring water.
== Subordinate Shrines == [[File:Oomiwa-jinja (tochigishi) jingu.JPG|thumb|200px|Jingū: houses the aidadono (shared) deities of the main shrine]] There are 15 shrine buildings in total:

'''Muro no Yashima''' {{div col}} * Sengen Jinja * Futarayama Jinja * Tsukuba Jinja * Raiden Jinja * Katori Jinja * Kashima Jinja * Kumano Jinja * Tenman-gū {{div col end}}

== Cultural Properties == === Tochigi City Designated Intangible Folk Cultural Properties === * Kagura of Ōmiwa Jinja - designated May 19, 1964 * Hoko (Spear) festival of Ōmiwa Jinja - designated May 19, 1964

{{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to a whole [[:en:Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[:en:Nara period|Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.<ref name="Herbert">{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}}</ref>
Whenever a new [[:en:Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,<ref name="Bocking">{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}}</ref>
The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[:en:Inaba|Inaba]]. <ref name="Hardacre">{{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}}</ref>
The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[:en:Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[:en:Okayama Prefecture|Okayama Prefecture]].
==Japanese content== '''Ōmiwa Jinja''' (大神神社, also romanized as Oomiwa Jinja) is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] located in Sōja-chō, [[:en:Tochigi (city)|Tochigi City]], [[:en:Tochigi Prefecture|Tochigi Prefecture]], Japan. It is a possible match (ronsha) for a "Shikinaisha" (small) recorded in historical texts, and is known as the Sōja (total shrine) of Shimotsuke Province. Under the modern shrine Rank system of the Meiji era, it was classified as a Prefectural Shrine. Historically, it was also known by other names such as "Shimotsuke Sōja Daimyōjin," "Sōja Rokusho Daimyōjin," and "Muroyashima Sōja Daimyōjin."
During the Ritsuryō era, the provincial capital (kokufu) was located about 2 km south of the shrine. Ōmiwa Jinja served as the sōja of that kokufu, and the local place name “Sōja” is derived from this shrine.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.city.tochigi.lg.jp/uploaded/attachment/55689.pdf|title=Chapter 2: Historical Scenery of Tochigi City to be Maintained and Improved |website=Tochigi City|accessdate=2024-11-11|page=177}}</ref>
The shrine is also known for the "Muro no Yashima" (Muro no Yashima) mentioned in Matsuo Bashō’s famous travelogue, the "Oku no Hosomichi."
== Deities Enshrined == '''Principal deity:''' * *Yamato-Ōmononushi-Kushi-mikatama no Mikoto* (倭大物主櫛𤭖玉命)<ref>According to the shrine's official literature.</ref> : In the "Izumo no Kuni no Miyatsuko Kamuyogoto," this refers to Ōmononushi no Kami. The deity is said to be an offshoot of the Ōmiwa Jinja (大神神社) in Sakurai City, Nara Prefecture. During Emperor Sujin’s reign, suffering from natural disasters and plagues, the emperor had a dream in which the deity Ōmononushi appeared and gave instructions. Following them, a man named Ootataneko performed rites at Mount Miwa, resulting in the cessation of calamities and epidemics. This story is recorded in the "Nihon Shoki."
'''Additional Deities (Aiadono-matsuri):''' * Kono-hanasakuya-hime (木花咲耶姫命) * Ninigi no Mikoto (瓊々杵命), husband of Kono-hanasakuya-hime * Ōyamatsumi no Mikoto (大山祇命), father of Kono-hanasakuya-hime * Hikohohodemi no Mikoto (彦火々出見命), child of Kono-hanasakuya-hime
== History == === Founding === According to shrine tradition, during Emperor Sujin's era, Prince Toyokiirihiko (豊城入彦命), while subjugating the eastern provinces, prayed for victory and peace of mind at a place known as "Muro no Yashima." He is said to have enshrined the great deity of Ōmiwa (from the capital at Isonokami in Yamato) at this site, establishing the shrine.<ref name="由緒書">Shrine’s official literature.</ref>
=== Historical Overview === The mid-Heian period text "Engishiki Jinmyōchō" lists a “Ōgami Jinja” in Tsuga District, Shimotsuke Province. One theory identifies Ōmiwa Jinja with that shrine, making it a "ronsha" (disputed match).<ref>Another candidate is Taihei-san Jinja in Hirai-chō, Tochigi City.</ref>
In ancient times, provincial governors (kokushi) would visit all shrines in the province, starting with the ichinomiya. To streamline this, they established a sōja near the kokufu to collectively worship all regional deities. Ōmiwa Jinja is believed to have served as the sōja of Shimotsuke Province. About 2.8 km south, the ruins of the Shimotsuke Kokuchō (provincial government offices) have been excavated.
During the rebellion of Taira no Masakado (Heian period), the shrine suffered damage. Fujiwara no Hidesato and others helped rebuild it, and until the Muromachi period, it had grand buildings.<ref name="由緒書"/> However, during the Sengoku period, the remnants of Minagawa Hiroteru’s forces barricaded themselves in the shrine. Hōjō Ujinao’s army set it on fire, resulting in destruction and decline.<ref name="由緒書"/>
It was said that through contributions by Tokugawa Iemitsu, who donated 30 koku of land and 10,000 pine saplings, the shrine was rebuilt in 1682 (Tenna 2) to its current form.<ref name="由緒書"/>
However, no historical documents prior to the Meiji era have been found that clearly refer to this shrine as “Ōmiwa (Ōmiwa)” or “Ōmiwa.” One theory suggests that a deity from Ōmiwa Jinja (Ōmiwa Jinja in Yamato) was worshiped at another location and later merged at the Sōja of Shimotsuke.<ref>On-site information board.</ref>
After the Meiji Restoration, in Meiji 6 (1873), the shrine was Ranked as a Gōsha (village shrine) under the modern shrine Ranking system.<ref name="由緒書"/> In Meiji 40 (1907), it was designated a shrine entitled to government offerings (Shinsen Heihaku Ryō Kyōshin Jinja), and in Meiji 44 (1911), it was promoted to Prefectural Shrine. Major renovations took place in 1924 (Taishō 13) and 1993 (Heisei 5). The Kuniho family traditionally served as hereditary Ōmiya-gūji (chief priests).
=== Shinhonors (Shinkai)=== * On August 29, Genkei 4 (880), it was elevated from Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade to Senior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade in the "Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku." The recorded deity name is "Miwa no Kami (三和神)"—some believe this refers to this shrine.<ref name="地名">"Tochigi-ken no Chimei" (Heibonsha) entry on Ōmiwa Jinja.</ref>
== Precincts == === Shrine Buildings === <gallery widths="200px" heights="150px"> File:Oomiwa-jinja (tochigishi) honden.JPG|Honden File:Oomiwa-jinja (tochigishi) haiden.JPG|Haiden File:Oomiwa-jinja (tochigishi) kaguraden.JPG|Kagura-den </gallery>
=== Sanctuary Forest === The forested area around Ōmiwa Jinja is designated as the Sōja Greenery Conservation Area by Tochigi Prefecture.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.pref.tochigi.lg.jp/d04/30jikannti/12souja.html|title=12 Sōja Greenery Environmental Conservation Area|website=Tochigi Prefecture|accessdate=2024-11-11}}</ref>
=== Muro no Yashima === [[File:Oomiwa-jinja (tochigishi) muronoyashima.JPG|thumb|200px|Muro no Yashima]] [[File:TochigiOhmiwaShine2.JPG|thumb|200px|Bashō’s haiku monument before Muro no Yashima]] "Muro no Yashima" has long been known as a utamakura (poetic place name) in classical Japanese poetry. The island in the shrine’s pond is said to be its location (though some argue this is a later association).<ref>See Kōjien, "Muro no Yashima." (Kotobank [https://kotobank.jp/word/%E5%AE%A4%E3%81%AE%E5%85%AB%E5%B3%B6-642624 article])</ref> It has been mentioned since the Nara period and appears in anthologies like the "Man’yōshū" and "Kokin Wakashū."
Famous poems: * Fujiwara no Sanekata (Shika Wakashū) * Minamoto no Shigeyuki’s daughter (Zoku Goshūi Wakashū) * Ōe no Masafusa (Shinshūi Wakashū) * Fujiwara no Shunzei (Chōshū Eiso) * Fujiwara no Teika (Shin Chokusen Wakashū)
Meanings associated with Muro no Yashima: * A site of a myth where Konohanasakuya-hime proved her chastity by setting herself aflame inside a room. * Possibly relates to a hearth’s smoke, turning into metaphorical love’s burning flame. * The marshy Omoigawa River basin producing water vapor or rising mist. * Over time associated with passionate love, smoke, and even kagerō (heat haze or spider’s thread).
Matsuo Bashō and his companion Sora mention Muro no Yashima in "Oku no Hosomichi," but they did not include a haiku in the main text. However, in Sora’s “Haikai Kakinotame,” one of Bashō’s verses “ito asobi ni musubitsukitaru keburi kana” ("Oh, the smoke that has tied itself to the thread playing in the air!") is recorded. This haiku is inscribed on a monument erected in 1869 (Meiji 2) by the late Edo period haijin Kōun Kaku Shunpō, with calligraphy by Hagiwara Shūgan, an Edo-period calligrapher.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Tochigi Inishie no Kairō: History of Cultural Properties |url=https://www.inishie.tochigi.jp/detail.html?course_id=5&id=0|accessdate=2024-02-22}}</ref>
Today’s Muro no Yashima is about 800 tsubo (approx. 2,640 square meters) of landscaped garden featuring eight small islands with small shrines dedicated to various prominent deities, including Tsukuba, Tenman, Kashima, Raiden, Sengen, Kumano, Futarayama, and Katori. There is no visible water vapor or spring water.
== Subordinate Shrines == [[File:Oomiwa-jinja (tochigishi) jingu.JPG|thumb|200px|Jingū: houses the aidadono (shared) deities of the main shrine]] There are 15 shrine buildings in total:
{{div col}} * Jingū * Gokoku Jinja * Fukujin Jinja * Ōsugi Jinja * Soreisha * Samon Jinja * Umon Jinja {{div col end}}
'''Muro no Yashima''' {{div col}} * Sengen Jinja * Futarayama Jinja * Tsukuba Jinja * Raiden Jinja * Katori Jinja * Kashima Jinja * Kumano Jinja * Tenman-gū {{div col end}}
== festivals == * Gantan-sai (January 1st) * New Year’s Pilgrimage and Shinshun Kigan-sai (January) * Setsubun-sai and Tsuina-shiki (February 3rd) * Kinen-sai (February 25th) * Chinka-sai (Early March) * Spring Grand festival (April 16th) - Includes yabusame (horseback archery) * Hatsu-uma-sai (on the first Uma day in May) * Ōharae (June 30th) * Yashima-sai (August 1st) * Ōsugi-sai, Kaze-matsuri (Mid-August) * Shichi-go-san visits (November 15th) * Autumn Grand festival (Mikoshi festival) (around November 18-24)
== Cultural Properties == === Tochigi City Designated Intangible Folk Cultural Properties === * Kagura of Ōmiwa Jinja - designated May 19, 1964 * Hoko (Spear) festival of Ōmiwa Jinja - designated May 19, 1964
=== Historic Sites === * Tochigi City Designated Historic Site "Shimotsuke Sōja (Muro no Yashima)" - designated February 16, 1968
== location == * location: Sōja-chō 477, Tochigi City, Tochigi Prefecture == Access == * About 15 minutes’ walk from Yashū-Ōtsuka Station on the Tōbu Utsunomiya Line
== Surrounding Area == * Shimotsuke Kokuchō Ruins approx. 2.8 km south

== Precincts == === Shrine Buildings === <gallery widths="200px" heights="150px"> File:Oomiwa-jinja (tochigishi) honden.JPG|Honden File:Oomiwa-jinja (tochigishi) haiden.JPG|Haiden File:Oomiwa-jinja (tochigishi) kaguraden.JPG|Kagura-den </gallery>
=== Sanctuary Forest === The forested area around Ōmiwa Jinja is designated as the Sōja Greenery Conservation Area by Tochigi Prefecture.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.pref.tochigi.lg.jp/d04/30jikannti/12souja.html|title=12 Sōja Greenery Environmental Conservation Area|website=Tochigi Prefecture|accessdate=2024-11-11}}</ref>
=== Muro no Yashima === [[File:Oomiwa-jinja (tochigishi) muronoyashima.JPG|thumb|200px|Muro no Yashima]] [[File:TochigiOhmiwaShine2.JPG|thumb|200px|Bashō’s haiku monument before Muro no Yashima]] "Muro no Yashima" has long been known as a utamakura (poetic place name) in classical Japanese poetry. The island in the shrine’s pond is said to be its location (though some argue this is a later association).<ref>See Kōjien, "Muro no Yashima." (Kotobank [https://kotobank.jp/word/%E5%AE%A4%E3%81%AE%E5%85%AB%E5%B3%B6-642624 article])</ref> It has been mentioned since the Nara period and appears in anthologies like the "Man’yōshū" and "Kokin Wakashū."
Famous poems: * Fujiwara no Sanekata (Shika Wakashū) * Minamoto no Shigeyuki’s daughter (Zoku Goshūi Wakashū) * Ōe no Masafusa (Shinshūi Wakashū) * Fujiwara no Shunzei (Chōshū Eiso) * Fujiwara no Teika (Shin Chokusen Wakashū)
Meanings associated with Muro no Yashima: * A site of a myth where Konohanasakuya-hime proved her chastity by setting herself aflame inside a room. * Possibly relates to a hearth’s smoke, turning into metaphorical love’s burning flame. * The marshy Omoigawa River basin producing water vapor or rising mist. * Over time associated with passionate love, smoke, and even kagerō (heat haze or spider’s thread).
Matsuo Bashō and his companion Sora mention Muro no Yashima in "Oku no Hosomichi," but they did not include a haiku in the main text. However, in Sora’s “Haikai Kakinotame,” one of Bashō’s verses “ito asobi ni musubitsukitaru keburi kana” ("Oh, the smoke that has tied itself to the thread playing in the air!") is recorded. This haiku is inscribed on a monument erected in 1869 (Meiji 2) by the late Edo period haijin Kōun Kaku Shunpō, with calligraphy by Hagiwara Shūgan, an Edo-period calligrapher.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Tochigi Inishie no Kairō: History of Cultural Properties |url=https://www.inishie.tochigi.jp/detail.html?course_id=5&id=0|accessdate=2024-02-22}}</ref>
Today’s Muro no Yashima is about 800 tsubo (approx. 2,640 square meters) of landscaped garden featuring eight small islands with small shrines dedicated to various prominent deities, including Tsukuba, Tenman, Kashima, Raiden, Sengen, Kumano, Futarayama, and Katori. There is no visible water vapor or spring water.
== Subordinate Shrines == [[File:Oomiwa-jinja (tochigishi) jingu.JPG|thumb|200px|Jingū: houses the aidadono (shared) deities of the main shrine]] There are 15 shrine buildings in total:
{{div col}} * Jingū * Gokoku Jinja * Fukujin Jinja * Ōsugi Jinja * Soreisha * Samon Jinja * Umon Jinja {{div col end}}
'''Muro no Yashima''' {{div col}} * Sengen Jinja * Futarayama Jinja * Tsukuba Jinja * Raiden Jinja * Katori Jinja * Kashima Jinja * Kumano Jinja * Tenman-gū {{div col end}}
== festivals == * Gantan-sai (January 1st) * New Year’s Pilgrimage and Shinshun Kigan-sai (January) * Setsubun-sai and Tsuina-shiki (February 3rd) * Kinen-sai (February 25th) * Chinka-sai (Early March) * Spring Grand festival (April 16th) - Includes yabusame (horseback archery) * Hatsu-uma-sai (on the first Uma day in May) * Ōharae (June 30th) * Yashima-sai (August 1st) * Ōsugi-sai, Kaze-matsuri (Mid-August) * Shichi-go-san visits (November 15th) * Autumn Grand festival (Mikoshi festival) (around November 18-24)
== Cultural Properties == === Tochigi City Designated Intangible Folk Cultural Properties === * Kagura of Ōmiwa Jinja - designated May 19, 1964 * Hoko (Spear) festival of Ōmiwa Jinja - designated May 19, 1964
=== Historic Sites === * Tochigi City Designated Historic Site "Shimotsuke Sōja (Muro no Yashima)" - designated February 16, 1968
== location == * location: Sōja-chō 477, Tochigi City, Tochigi Prefecture == Access == * About 15 minutes’ walk from Yashū-Ōtsuka Station on the Tōbu Utsunomiya Line
== Surrounding Area == * Shimotsuke Kokuchō Ruins approx. 2.8 km south

{{Distinguish|Omiwa Shrine}} {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | image = File:Oomiwa-jinja (tochigishi) torii.JPG | deity = {{ill|Ōmononushi|qid=Q10936701}} | type = [[Sōja shrine|Sōja shrine]] |religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Ōmiwa Jinja (Oomiwa Shrine) | caption = | map_type = Japan Tochigi | coordinates = {{Coord|36.4059167|N|139.7821556|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | location = Sōja-chō 477, [[:en:Tochigi (city)|Tochigi City]], [[:en:Tochigi Prefecture|Tochigi Prefecture]] | type = Shikinaisha (small), a disputed identification (ronsha), Sōja of Shimotsuke Province, Former Prefectural Shrine | founded = (Trad.) 48th year of Emperor Sujin’s reign | festival = November 18–26 | location = {{ill|Tochigi|qid=Q44830}} }} {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine (Shimotsuke)|lt=Ōmiwa Jinja|ja|大神神社 (栃木市)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōmiwa Shrine (Shimotsuke)|qq=}} is a [[Sōja shrine|Sōja shrine]]. It enshrines all the [[kami]] of the shrines in [[:en:Shimotsuke Province|Shimotsuke Province]]
Ichinomiya and Soja are not the same thing but were sometimes combined<ref>https://archive.ph/wip/XtZfZ</ref>
{{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to a whole [[:en:Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[:en:Nara period|Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.<ref name="Herbert">{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}}</ref>
Whenever a new [[:en:Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,<ref name="Bocking">{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}}</ref>
The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[:en:Inaba|Inaba]]. <ref name="Hardacre">{{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}}</ref>
The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[:en:Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[:en:Okayama Prefecture|Okayama Prefecture]].
==Japanese content== '''Ōmiwa Jinja''' (大神神社, also romanized as Oomiwa Jinja) is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] located in Sōja-chō, [[:en:Tochigi (city)|Tochigi City]], [[:en:Tochigi Prefecture|Tochigi Prefecture]], Japan. It is a possible match (ronsha) for a "Shikinaisha" (small) recorded in historical texts, and is known as the Sōja (total shrine) of Shimotsuke Province. Under the modern shrine Rank system of the Meiji era, it was classified as a Prefectural Shrine. Historically, it was also known by other names such as "Shimotsuke Sōja Daimyōjin," "Sōja Rokusho Daimyōjin," and "Muroyashima Sōja Daimyōjin."
During the Ritsuryō era, the provincial capital (kokufu) was located about 2 km south of the shrine. Ōmiwa Jinja served as the sōja of that kokufu, and the local place name “Sōja” is derived from this shrine.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.city.tochigi.lg.jp/uploaded/attachment/55689.pdf|title=Chapter 2: Historical Scenery of Tochigi City to be Maintained and Improved |website=Tochigi City|accessdate=2024-11-11|page=177}}</ref>
The shrine is also known for the "Muro no Yashima" (Muro no Yashima) mentioned in Matsuo Bashō’s famous travelogue, the "Oku no Hosomichi."
== Deities Enshrined == '''Principal deity:''' * *Yamato-Ōmononushi-Kushi-mikatama no Mikoto* (倭大物主櫛𤭖玉命)<ref>According to the shrine's official literature.</ref> : In the "Izumo no Kuni no Miyatsuko Kamuyogoto," this refers to Ōmononushi no Kami. The deity is said to be an offshoot of the Ōmiwa Jinja (大神神社) in Sakurai City, Nara Prefecture. During Emperor Sujin’s reign, suffering from natural disasters and plagues, the emperor had a dream in which the deity Ōmononushi appeared and gave instructions. Following them, a man named Ootataneko performed rites at Mount Miwa, resulting in the cessation of calamities and epidemics. This story is recorded in the "Nihon Shoki."
'''Additional Deities (Aiadono-matsuri):''' * Kono-hanasakuya-hime (木花咲耶姫命) * Ninigi no Mikoto (瓊々杵命), husband of Kono-hanasakuya-hime * Ōyamatsumi no Mikoto (大山祇命), father of Kono-hanasakuya-hime * Hikohohodemi no Mikoto (彦火々出見命), child of Kono-hanasakuya-hime
== History == === Founding === According to shrine tradition, during Emperor Sujin's era, Prince Toyokiirihiko (豊城入彦命), while subjugating the eastern provinces, prayed for victory and peace of mind at a place known as "Muro no Yashima." He is said to have enshrined the great deity of Ōmiwa (from the capital at Isonokami in Yamato) at this site, establishing the shrine.<ref name="由緒書">Shrine’s official literature.</ref>
=== Historical Overview === The mid-Heian period text "Engishiki Jinmyōchō" lists a “Ōgami Jinja” in Tsuga District, Shimotsuke Province. One theory identifies Ōmiwa Jinja with that shrine, making it a "ronsha" (disputed match).<ref>Another candidate is Taihei-san Jinja in Hirai-chō, Tochigi City.</ref>
In ancient times, provincial governors (kokushi) would visit all shrines in the province, starting with the ichinomiya. To streamline this, they established a sōja near the kokufu to collectively worship all regional deities. Ōmiwa Jinja is believed to have served as the sōja of Shimotsuke Province. About 2.8 km south, the ruins of the Shimotsuke Kokuchō (provincial government offices) have been excavated.
During the rebellion of Taira no Masakado (Heian period), the shrine suffered damage. Fujiwara no Hidesato and others helped rebuild it, and until the Muromachi period, it had grand buildings.<ref name="由緒書"/> However, during the Sengoku period, the remnants of Minagawa Hiroteru’s forces barricaded themselves in the shrine. Hōjō Ujinao’s army set it on fire, resulting in destruction and decline.<ref name="由緒書"/>
It was said that through contributions by Tokugawa Iemitsu, who donated 30 koku of land and 10,000 pine saplings, the shrine was rebuilt in 1682 (Tenna 2) to its current form.<ref name="由緒書"/>
However, no historical documents prior to the Meiji era have been found that clearly refer to this shrine as “Ōmiwa (Ōmiwa)” or “Ōmiwa.” One theory suggests that a deity from Ōmiwa Jinja (Ōmiwa Jinja in Yamato) was worshiped at another location and later merged at the Sōja of Shimotsuke.<ref>On-site information board.</ref>
After the Meiji Restoration, in Meiji 6 (1873), the shrine was Ranked as a Gōsha (village shrine) under the modern shrine Ranking system.<ref name="由緒書"/> In Meiji 40 (1907), it was designated a shrine entitled to government offerings (Shinsen Heihaku Ryō Kyōshin Jinja), and in Meiji 44 (1911), it was promoted to Prefectural Shrine. Major renovations took place in 1924 (Taishō 13) and 1993 (Heisei 5). The Kuniho family traditionally served as hereditary Ōmiya-gūji (chief priests).
=== Shinhonors (Shinkai)=== * On August 29, Genkei 4 (880), it was elevated from Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade to Senior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade in the "Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku." The recorded deity name is "Miwa no Kami (三和神)"—some believe this refers to this shrine.<ref name="地名">"Tochigi-ken no Chimei" (Heibonsha) entry on Ōmiwa Jinja.</ref>

It enshrines all the [[kami]] of the shrines in [[:en:Shimotsuke Province|Shimotsuke Province]]
Ichinomiya and Soja are not the same thing but were sometimes combined<ref>https://archive.ph/wip/XtZfZ</ref>
{{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to a whole [[:en:Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[:en:Nara period|Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.<ref name="Herbert">{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}}</ref>
Whenever a new [[:en:Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,<ref name="Bocking">{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}}</ref>
The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[:en:Inaba|Inaba]]. <ref name="Hardacre">{{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}}</ref>
The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[:en:Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[:en:Okayama Prefecture|Okayama Prefecture]].
==Japanese content== '''Ōmiwa Jinja''' (大神神社, also romanized as Oomiwa Jinja) is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] located in Sōja-chō, [[:en:Tochigi (city)|Tochigi City]], [[:en:Tochigi Prefecture|Tochigi Prefecture]], Japan. It is a possible match (ronsha) for a "Shikinaisha" (small) recorded in historical texts, and is known as the Sōja (total shrine) of Shimotsuke Province. Under the modern shrine Rank system of the Meiji era, it was classified as a Prefectural Shrine. Historically, it was also known by other names such as "Shimotsuke Sōja Daimyōjin," "Sōja Rokusho Daimyōjin," and "Muroyashima Sōja Daimyōjin."
During the Ritsuryō era, the provincial capital (kokufu) was located about 2 km south of the shrine. Ōmiwa Jinja served as the sōja of that kokufu, and the local place name “Sōja” is derived from this shrine.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.city.tochigi.lg.jp/uploaded/attachment/55689.pdf|title=Chapter 2: Historical Scenery of Tochigi City to be Maintained and Improved |website=Tochigi City|accessdate=2024-11-11|page=177}}</ref>
The shrine is also known for the "Muro no Yashima" (Muro no Yashima) mentioned in Matsuo Bashō’s famous travelogue, the "Oku no Hosomichi."
== Deities Enshrined == '''Principal deity:''' * *Yamato-Ōmononushi-Kushi-mikatama no Mikoto* (倭大物主櫛𤭖玉命)<ref>According to the shrine's official literature.</ref> : In the "Izumo no Kuni no Miyatsuko Kamuyogoto," this refers to Ōmononushi no Kami. The deity is said to be an offshoot of the Ōmiwa Jinja (大神神社) in Sakurai City, Nara Prefecture. During Emperor Sujin’s reign, suffering from natural disasters and plagues, the emperor had a dream in which the deity Ōmononushi appeared and gave instructions. Following them, a man named Ootataneko performed rites at Mount Miwa, resulting in the cessation of calamities and epidemics. This story is recorded in the "Nihon Shoki."
'''Additional Deities (Aiadono-matsuri):''' * Kono-hanasakuya-hime (木花咲耶姫命) * Ninigi no Mikoto (瓊々杵命), husband of Kono-hanasakuya-hime * Ōyamatsumi no Mikoto (大山祇命), father of Kono-hanasakuya-hime * Hikohohodemi no Mikoto (彦火々出見命), child of Kono-hanasakuya-hime
== History == === Founding === According to shrine tradition, during Emperor Sujin's era, Prince Toyokiirihiko (豊城入彦命), while subjugating the eastern provinces, prayed for victory and peace of mind at a place known as "Muro no Yashima." He is said to have enshrined the great deity of Ōmiwa (from the capital at Isonokami in Yamato) at this site, establishing the shrine.<ref name="由緒書">Shrine’s official literature.</ref>
=== Historical Overview === The mid-Heian period text "Engishiki Jinmyōchō" lists a “Ōgami Jinja” in Tsuga District, Shimotsuke Province. One theory identifies Ōmiwa Jinja with that shrine, making it a "ronsha" (disputed match).<ref>Another candidate is Taihei-san Jinja in Hirai-chō, Tochigi City.</ref>
In ancient times, provincial governors (kokushi) would visit all shrines in the province, starting with the ichinomiya. To streamline this, they established a sōja near the kokufu to collectively worship all regional deities. Ōmiwa Jinja is believed to have served as the sōja of Shimotsuke Province. About 2.8 km south, the ruins of the Shimotsuke Kokuchō (provincial government offices) have been excavated.
During the rebellion of Taira no Masakado (Heian period), the shrine suffered damage. Fujiwara no Hidesato and others helped rebuild it, and until the Muromachi period, it had grand buildings.<ref name="由緒書"/> However, during the Sengoku period, the remnants of Minagawa Hiroteru’s forces barricaded themselves in the shrine. Hōjō Ujinao’s army set it on fire, resulting in destruction and decline.<ref name="由緒書"/>
It was said that through contributions by Tokugawa Iemitsu, who donated 30 koku of land and 10,000 pine saplings, the shrine was rebuilt in 1682 (Tenna 2) to its current form.<ref name="由緒書"/>
However, no historical documents prior to the Meiji era have been found that clearly refer to this shrine as “Ōmiwa (Ōmiwa)” or “Ōmiwa.” One theory suggests that a deity from Ōmiwa Jinja (Ōmiwa Jinja in Yamato) was worshiped at another location and later merged at the Sōja of Shimotsuke.<ref>On-site information board.</ref>
After the Meiji Restoration, in Meiji 6 (1873), the shrine was Ranked as a Gōsha (village shrine) under the modern shrine Ranking system.<ref name="由緒書"/> In Meiji 40 (1907), it was designated a shrine entitled to government offerings (Shinsen Heihaku Ryō Kyōshin Jinja), and in Meiji 44 (1911), it was promoted to Prefectural Shrine. Major renovations took place in 1924 (Taishō 13) and 1993 (Heisei 5). The Kuniho family traditionally served as hereditary Ōmiya-gūji (chief priests).
=== Shinhonors (Shinkai)=== * On August 29, Genkei 4 (880), it was elevated from Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade to Senior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade in the "Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku." The recorded deity name is "Miwa no Kami (三和神)"—some believe this refers to this shrine.<ref name="地名">"Tochigi-ken no Chimei" (Heibonsha) entry on Ōmiwa Jinja.</ref>
== Precincts == === Shrine Buildings === <gallery widths="200px" heights="150px"> File:Oomiwa-jinja (tochigishi) honden.JPG|Honden File:Oomiwa-jinja (tochigishi) haiden.JPG|Haiden File:Oomiwa-jinja (tochigishi) kaguraden.JPG|Kagura-den </gallery>
=== Sanctuary Forest === The forested area around Ōmiwa Jinja is designated as the Sōja Greenery Conservation Area by Tochigi Prefecture.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.pref.tochigi.lg.jp/d04/30jikannti/12souja.html|title=12 Sōja Greenery Environmental Conservation Area|website=Tochigi Prefecture|accessdate=2024-11-11}}</ref>
=== Muro no Yashima === [[File:Oomiwa-jinja (tochigishi) muronoyashima.JPG|thumb|200px|Muro no Yashima]] [[File:TochigiOhmiwaShine2.JPG|thumb|200px|Bashō’s haiku monument before Muro no Yashima]] "Muro no Yashima" has long been known as a utamakura (poetic place name) in classical Japanese poetry. The island in the shrine’s pond is said to be its location (though some argue this is a later association).<ref>See Kōjien, "Muro no Yashima." (Kotobank [https://kotobank.jp/word/%E5%AE%A4%E3%81%AE%E5%85%AB%E5%B3%B6-642624 article])</ref> It has been mentioned since the Nara period and appears in anthologies like the "Man’yōshū" and "Kokin Wakashū."
Famous poems: * Fujiwara no Sanekata (Shika Wakashū) * Minamoto no Shigeyuki’s daughter (Zoku Goshūi Wakashū) * Ōe no Masafusa (Shinshūi Wakashū) * Fujiwara no Shunzei (Chōshū Eiso) * Fujiwara no Teika (Shin Chokusen Wakashū)
Meanings associated with Muro no Yashima: * A site of a myth where Konohanasakuya-hime proved her chastity by setting herself aflame inside a room. * Possibly relates to a hearth’s smoke, turning into metaphorical love’s burning flame. * The marshy Omoigawa River basin producing water vapor or rising mist. * Over time associated with passionate love, smoke, and even kagerō (heat haze or spider’s thread).
Matsuo Bashō and his companion Sora mention Muro no Yashima in "Oku no Hosomichi," but they did not include a haiku in the main text. However, in Sora’s “Haikai Kakinotame,” one of Bashō’s verses “ito asobi ni musubitsukitaru keburi kana” ("Oh, the smoke that has tied itself to the thread playing in the air!") is recorded. This haiku is inscribed on a monument erected in 1869 (Meiji 2) by the late Edo period haijin Kōun Kaku Shunpō, with calligraphy by Hagiwara Shūgan, an Edo-period calligrapher.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Tochigi Inishie no Kairō: History of Cultural Properties |url=https://www.inishie.tochigi.jp/detail.html?course_id=5&id=0|accessdate=2024-02-22}}</ref>
Today’s Muro no Yashima is about 800 tsubo (approx. 2,640 square meters) of landscaped garden featuring eight small islands with small shrines dedicated to various prominent deities, including Tsukuba, Tenman, Kashima, Raiden, Sengen, Kumano, Futarayama, and Katori. There is no visible water vapor or spring water.
== Subordinate Shrines == [[File:Oomiwa-jinja (tochigishi) jingu.JPG|thumb|200px|Jingū: houses the aidadono (shared) deities of the main shrine]] There are 15 shrine buildings in total:
{{div col}} * Jingū * Gokoku Jinja * Fukujin Jinja * Ōsugi Jinja * Soreisha * Samon Jinja * Umon Jinja {{div col end}}
'''Muro no Yashima''' {{div col}} * Sengen Jinja * Futarayama Jinja * Tsukuba Jinja * Raiden Jinja * Katori Jinja * Kashima Jinja * Kumano Jinja * Tenman-gū {{div col end}}
== festivals == * Gantan-sai (January 1st) * New Year’s Pilgrimage and Shinshun Kigan-sai (January) * Setsubun-sai and Tsuina-shiki (February 3rd) * Kinen-sai (February 25th) * Chinka-sai (Early March) * Spring Grand festival (April 16th) - Includes yabusame (horseback archery) * Hatsu-uma-sai (on the first Uma day in May) * Ōharae (June 30th) * Yashima-sai (August 1st) * Ōsugi-sai, Kaze-matsuri (Mid-August) * Shichi-go-san visits (November 15th) * Autumn Grand festival (Mikoshi festival) (around November 18-24)
== Cultural Properties == === Tochigi City Designated Intangible Folk Cultural Properties === * Kagura of Ōmiwa Jinja - designated May 19, 1964 * Hoko (Spear) festival of Ōmiwa Jinja - designated May 19, 1964
=== Historic Sites === * Tochigi City Designated Historic Site "Shimotsuke Sōja (Muro no Yashima)" - designated February 16, 1968
== location == * location: Sōja-chō 477, Tochigi City, Tochigi Prefecture == Access == * About 15 minutes’ walk from Yashū-Ōtsuka Station on the Tōbu Utsunomiya Line
== Surrounding Area == * Shimotsuke Kokuchō Ruins approx. 2.8 km south

One theory identifies Ōmiwa Jinja with that shrine, making it a "ronsha" (disputed match).<ref>Another candidate is Taihei-san Jinja in Hirai-chō, Tochigi City.</ref>
In ancient times, provincial governors (kokushi) would visit all shrines in the province, starting with the ichinomiya. To streamline this, they established a sōja near the kokufu to collectively worship all regional deities. Ōmiwa Jinja is believed to have served as the sōja of Shimotsuke Province. About 2.8 km south, the ruins of the Shimotsuke Kokuchō (provincial government offices) have been excavated.
During the rebellion of Taira no Masakado (Heian period), the shrine suffered damage. Fujiwara no Hidesato and others helped rebuild it, and until the Muromachi period, it had grand buildings.<ref name="由緒書"/> However, during the Sengoku period, the remnants of Minagawa Hiroteru’s forces barricaded themselves in the shrine. Hōjō Ujinao’s army set it on fire, resulting in destruction and decline.<ref name="由緒書"/>
It was said that through contributions by Tokugawa Iemitsu, who donated 30 koku of land and 10,000 pine saplings, the shrine was rebuilt in 1682 (Tenna 2) to its current form.<ref name="由緒書"/>
However, no historical documents prior to the Meiji era have been found that clearly refer to this shrine as “Ōmiwa (Ōmiwa)” or “Ōmiwa.” One theory suggests that a deity from Ōmiwa Jinja (Ōmiwa Jinja in Yamato) was worshiped at another location and later merged at the Sōja of Shimotsuke.<ref>On-site information board.</ref>
After the Meiji Restoration, in Meiji 6 (1873), the shrine was Ranked as a Gōsha (village shrine) under the modern shrine Ranking system.<ref name="由緒書"/> In Meiji 40 (1907), it was designated a shrine entitled to government offerings (Shinsen Heihaku Ryō Kyōshin Jinja), and in Meiji 44 (1911), it was promoted to Prefectural Shrine. Major renovations took place in 1924 (Taishō 13) and 1993 (Heisei 5). The Kuniho family traditionally served as hereditary Ōmiya-gūji (chief priests).
=== Shinhonors (Shinkai)=== * On August 29, Genkei 4 (880), it was elevated from Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade to Senior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade in the "Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku." The recorded deity name is "Miwa no Kami (三和神)"—some believe this refers to this shrine.<ref name="地名">"Tochigi-ken no Chimei" (Heibonsha) entry on Ōmiwa Jinja.</ref>
== Precincts == === Shrine Buildings === <gallery widths="200px" heights="150px"> File:Oomiwa-jinja (tochigishi) honden.JPG|Honden File:Oomiwa-jinja (tochigishi) haiden.JPG|Haiden File:Oomiwa-jinja (tochigishi) kaguraden.JPG|Kagura-den </gallery>
=== Sanctuary Forest === The forested area around Ōmiwa Jinja is designated as the Sōja Greenery Conservation Area by Tochigi Prefecture.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.pref.tochigi.lg.jp/d04/30jikannti/12souja.html|title=12 Sōja Greenery Environmental Conservation Area|website=Tochigi Prefecture|accessdate=2024-11-11}}</ref>
=== Muro no Yashima === [[File:Oomiwa-jinja (tochigishi) muronoyashima.JPG|thumb|200px|Muro no Yashima]] [[File:TochigiOhmiwaShine2.JPG|thumb|200px|Bashō’s haiku monument before Muro no Yashima]] "Muro no Yashima" has long been known as a utamakura (poetic place name) in classical Japanese poetry. The island in the shrine’s pond is said to be its location (though some argue this is a later association).<ref>See Kōjien, "Muro no Yashima." (Kotobank [https://kotobank.jp/word/%E5%AE%A4%E3%81%AE%E5%85%AB%E5%B3%B6-642624 article])</ref> It has been mentioned since the Nara period and appears in anthologies like the "Man’yōshū" and "Kokin Wakashū."
Famous poems: * Fujiwara no Sanekata (Shika Wakashū) * Minamoto no Shigeyuki’s daughter (Zoku Goshūi Wakashū) * Ōe no Masafusa (Shinshūi Wakashū) * Fujiwara no Shunzei (Chōshū Eiso) * Fujiwara no Teika (Shin Chokusen Wakashū)
Meanings associated with Muro no Yashima: * A site of a myth where Konohanasakuya-hime proved her chastity by setting herself aflame inside a room. * Possibly relates to a hearth’s smoke, turning into metaphorical love’s burning flame. * The marshy Omoigawa River basin producing water vapor or rising mist. * Over time associated with passionate love, smoke, and even kagerō (heat haze or spider’s thread).
Matsuo Bashō and his companion Sora mention Muro no Yashima in "Oku no Hosomichi," but they did not include a haiku in the main text. However, in Sora’s “Haikai Kakinotame,” one of Bashō’s verses “ito asobi ni musubitsukitaru keburi kana” ("Oh, the smoke that has tied itself to the thread playing in the air!") is recorded. This haiku is inscribed on a monument erected in 1869 (Meiji 2) by the late Edo period haijin Kōun Kaku Shunpō, with calligraphy by Hagiwara Shūgan, an Edo-period calligrapher.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Tochigi Inishie no Kairō: History of Cultural Properties |url=https://www.inishie.tochigi.jp/detail.html?course_id=5&id=0|accessdate=2024-02-22}}</ref>
Today’s Muro no Yashima is about 800 tsubo (approx. 2,640 square meters) of landscaped garden featuring eight small islands with small shrines dedicated to various prominent deities, including Tsukuba, Tenman, Kashima, Raiden, Sengen, Kumano, Futarayama, and Katori. There is no visible water vapor or spring water.

{{Distinguish|Omiwa Shrine}} {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | image = File:Oomiwa-jinja (tochigishi) torii.JPG | deity = {{ill|Ōmononushi|qid=Q10936701}} | type = [[Sōja shrine|Sōja shrine]] |religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Ōmiwa Jinja (Oomiwa Shrine) | caption = | map_type = Japan Tochigi | coordinates = {{Coord|36.4059167|N|139.7821556|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | location = Sōja-chō 477, [[:en:Tochigi (city)|Tochigi City]], [[:en:Tochigi Prefecture|Tochigi Prefecture]] | type = Shikinaisha (small), a disputed identification (ronsha), Sōja of Shimotsuke Province, Former Prefectural Shrine | founded = (Trad.) 48th year of Emperor Sujin’s reign | festival = November 18–26 | location = {{ill|Tochigi|qid=Q44830}} }} {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine (Shimotsuke)|lt=Ōmiwa Jinja|ja|大神神社 (栃木市)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōmiwa Shrine (Shimotsuke)|qq=}} is a [[Sōja shrine|Sōja shrine]]. It enshrines all the [[kami]] of the shrines in [[:en:Shimotsuke Province|Shimotsuke Province]]
Ichinomiya and Soja are not the same thing but were sometimes combined<ref>https://archive.ph/wip/XtZfZ</ref>
{{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to a whole [[:en:Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[:en:Nara period|Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.<ref name="Herbert">{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}}</ref>
Whenever a new [[:en:Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,<ref name="Bocking">{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}}</ref>
The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[:en:Inaba|Inaba]]. <ref name="Hardacre">{{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}}</ref>
The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[:en:Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[:en:Okayama Prefecture|Okayama Prefecture]].
==Japanese content== '''Ōmiwa Jinja''' (大神神社, also romanized as Oomiwa Jinja) is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] located in Sōja-chō, [[:en:Tochigi (city)|Tochigi City]], [[:en:Tochigi Prefecture|Tochigi Prefecture]], Japan. It is a possible match (ronsha) for a "Shikinaisha" (small) recorded in historical texts, and is known as the Sōja (total shrine) of Shimotsuke Province. Under the modern shrine Rank system of the Meiji era, it was classified as a Prefectural Shrine. Historically, it was also known by other names such as "Shimotsuke Sōja Daimyōjin," "Sōja Rokusho Daimyōjin," and "Muroyashima Sōja Daimyōjin."
During the Ritsuryō era, the provincial capital (kokufu) was located about 2 km south of the shrine. Ōmiwa Jinja served as the sōja of that kokufu, and the local place name “Sōja” is derived from this shrine.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.city.tochigi.lg.jp/uploaded/attachment/55689.pdf|title=Chapter 2: Historical Scenery of Tochigi City to be Maintained and Improved |website=Tochigi City|accessdate=2024-11-11|page=177}}</ref>
The shrine is also known for the "Muro no Yashima" (Muro no Yashima) mentioned in Matsuo Bashō’s famous travelogue, the "Oku no Hosomichi."
== Deities Enshrined == '''Principal deity:''' * *Yamato-Ōmononushi-Kushi-mikatama no Mikoto* (倭大物主櫛𤭖玉命)<ref>According to the shrine's official literature.</ref> : In the "Izumo no Kuni no Miyatsuko Kamuyogoto," this refers to Ōmononushi no Kami. The deity is said to be an offshoot of the Ōmiwa Jinja (大神神社) in Sakurai City, Nara Prefecture. During Emperor Sujin’s reign, suffering from natural disasters and plagues, the emperor had a dream in which the deity Ōmononushi appeared and gave instructions. Following them, a man named Ootataneko performed rites at Mount Miwa, resulting in the cessation of calamities and epidemics. This story is recorded in the "Nihon Shoki."
'''Additional Deities (Aiadono-matsuri):''' * Kono-hanasakuya-hime (木花咲耶姫命) * Ninigi no Mikoto (瓊々杵命), husband of Kono-hanasakuya-hime * Ōyamatsumi no Mikoto (大山祇命), father of Kono-hanasakuya-hime * Hikohohodemi no Mikoto (彦火々出見命), child of Kono-hanasakuya-hime
